quote: Configurations are not belief states. Their distinctness is an objective fact with experimental consequences. The configurations are distinct even if no one knows the state of S; distinct even if no intelligent entity can ever find out.
content: True, and less absolute than the essay’s “nailed in place, indivisible and unmergeable” suggests. The distinctness of two configurations that differ in the state of S is the overlap ⟨Sno|Syes⟩, a continuous quantity, and the interference at the detectors falls off continuously as that overlap shrinks; Englert’s duality relation (Englert (1996)) makes the tradeoff quantitative, fringe visibility squared plus path distinguishability squared at most one, and it has been measured across the whole range. The essay knows this (“if S were nudged, but S had an original spread... larger than the nudge”) and puts it in a parenthesis. The larger point it does not raise is that “the same configuration” is basis-relative: what the essay treats as the fixed set of configurations is the position basis, and the reason position is privileged for macroscopic objects is not that the laws nail it in place but that decoherence dynamically selects it, the einselection of a pointer basis by the interaction with the environment (Zurek (2003)). That is the substantive physics of the essay’s subject, and it is also where the Everettian “worlds” get their identity; presenting configurations as a discrete list fixed by fiat hides both the physics and the interpretive work.

quote: Though it is a little embarrassing that even after the theory of amplitudes and configurations had been worked out—with the theory now giving the definite prediction that any nudged particle would do the trick—early scientists still didn’t get it.
content: Some of them got it immediately, in print. Mott’s 1929 paper on the cloud chamber (Mott (1929)) asked why a spherical alpha-particle wave produces a straight track, and answered by treating the chamber’s atoms quantum-mechanically and showing that the joint amplitude for ionizing atoms not on a line vanishes; it is the first calculation of the kind the essay describes, and it is the ancestor of decoherence theory. Von Neumann’s 1932 book, the founding rigorous treatment, follows the measurement chain from the electron to the apparatus to the observer’s body and shows that the “cut” can be placed anywhere along it, which is the observation that the apparatus is “particles in different places”; he then adds the projection postulate as a separate process because the chain, followed to its end, yields no single outcome. The early scientists did not fail to notice that the apparatus was quantum; they noticed, worked it through, and found that noticing it did not by itself produce the definite results they saw. That is the measurement problem, and the essay’s history has them missing a point that their books are about. The claim that “you can still read this kind of stuff” about conscious observation in physics textbooks is also overstated: the standard graduate texts (Sakurai, Shankar, Griffiths) present measurement operationally and mention consciousness, if at all, to set it aside.
